lines.text: It is capstone time! Today you design and build your own turn-based Battle Arena game.
Each fighter is a dictionary, like {"name": "Goblin", "hp": 45}.
A list of enemy dictionaries lets random.choice pick a surprise opponent.
Changing enemy["hp"] changes that fighter’s health.
roll_damage, apply_damage and heal_hp each do one job and return a number. max(0, hp - damage) stops health going below zero. min(max_hp, hp + amount) stops healing above the maximum.
while player["hp"] > 0 and enemy["hp"] > 0: keeps the battle going.
Each turn shows the stats, asks for a move, and then the enemy strikes back.
When either health reaches zero, the loop ends.
After the loop, an if decides victory or defeat.
Then playtest it.
If the game is too easy or too hard, change the numbers: that is called balancing.
Every fighter keeps its stats in a dictionary, with the same keys for each one.
Random choice picks one enemy from the list, so every battle can be different.
Apply damage never lets health fall below zero, thanks to max.
Heal never goes above the maximum health, thanks to min.
The player chooses a move, and the program calls the right functions.
The damage is random, so every swing feels a little different.
The loop keeps going only while both fighters are still standing.
After the loop, one if statement decides whether you won or lost.
Game designers plan their fighters and numbers before writing any code.
Then they playtest again and again, and tweak the numbers until the battle feels fair.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now plan it, build it, test it, and share it!
